claim: Synaptophysins 1 and 2 and synaptogyrins 1 and 3 constitute a major family of synaptic vesicle membrane proteins.
source: Synaptophysins 1 and 2 and synaptogyrins 1 and 3 constitute a major family of synaptic vesicle membrane proteins.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by citations to prior literature (Jahn et al., 1985; Stenius, 1995; Fernández-Chacón and Südhof, 1999; Takamori et al., 2006) in the introduction.

claim: The primary function of synaptophysin family members has not been resolved.
source: Unlike other widely expressed synaptic vesicle proteins such as vSNAREs and synaptotagmins, the primary function has not been resolved.
evidence: This is a statement about the state of knowledge in the field, supported by the lack of consensus in prior literature.

claim: Quadruple knockout mice missing all four synaptophysin family members show robust elevation in the probability of release of readily releasable vesicles.
source: Here, we report robust elevation in the probability of release of readily releasable vesicles with both high and low release probabilities at a variety of synapse types from knockout mice missing all four family members.
evidence: This is the primary finding of the study, supported by experimental data presented in Figures 2-7.

claim: The number of readily releasable vesicles is not affected in quadruple knockout mice.
source: Neither the number of readily releasable vesicles, nor the timing of recruitment to the readily releasable pool was affected.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Figures 3-4 and 6-7.

claim: The timing of recruitment to the readily releasable pool is not affected in quadruple knockout mice.
source: Neither the number of readily releasable vesicles, nor the timing of recruitment to the readily releasable pool was affected.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Figures 3-4 and 6-7.

claim: Synaptophysin family members serve as negative regulators of neurotransmission.
source: The results suggest that family members serve as negative regulators of neurotransmission, acting directly at the level of exocytosis to dampen connection strength selectively when presynaptic action potentials fire at low frequency.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental findings, based on the observed increase in release probability in knockout mice.

claim: Synaptophysin family members act directly at the level of exocytosis.
source: The results suggest that family members serve as negative regulators of neurotransmission, acting directly at the level of exocytosis to dampen connection strength selectively when presynaptic action potentials fire at low frequency.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data showing elevated release probability without changes in vesicle recruitment or RRP size.

claim: Synaptophysin family members dampen connection strength selectively when presynaptic action potentials fire at low frequency.
source: The results suggest that family members serve as negative regulators of neurotransmission, acting directly at the level of exocytosis to dampen connection strength selectively when presynaptic action potentials fire at low frequency.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing differences at low frequency stimulation but not during high frequency steady state.

claim: Synaptophysin family members are expressed widely, possibly in all synaptic vesicles throughout the animal kingdom.
source: Synaptophysin 1 and 2 and synaptogyrin 1 and 3 constitute a major family of synaptic vesicle membrane proteins expressed widely, possibly in all synaptic vesicles throughout the animal kingdom (Jahn et al., 1985; Stenius, 1995; Fernández-Chacón and Südhof, 1999; Takamori et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Synaptogyrin 2, also known as cellugyrin, is non-neuronal.
source: Synaptogyrin 2, also known as cellugyrin, is non-neuronal (Janz and Südhof, 1998).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: Family members bind to the vSNARE synaptobrevin 2/VAMP 2.
source: Family members bind to the vSNARE synaptobrevin 2/VAMP 2, which is a core component of the machinery that catalyzes membrane fusion during synaptic vesicle exocytosis (Söllner et al., 1993; Calakos and Scheller, 1994; Washbourne et al., 1995; Edelmann et al., 1995; Becher et al., 1999; Khvotchev and Südhof, 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Synaptobrevin 2/VAMP 2 is a core component of the machinery that catalyzes membrane fusion during synaptic vesicle exocytosis.
source: Family members bind to the vSNARE synaptobrevin 2/VAMP 2, which is a core component of the machinery that catalyzes membrane fusion during synaptic vesicle exocytosis (Söllner et al., 1993; Calakos and Scheller, 1994; Washbourne et al., 1995; Edelmann et al., 1995; Becher et al., 1999; Khvotchev and Südhof, 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Overexpression of family members potently inhibited neurotransmitter release in a cell line.
source: And, overexpression of family members potently inhibited neurotransmitter release in a cell line (Sugita et al., 1999).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: No clear evidence was found for increases in neurotransmitter release at synapses from synaptophysin 1 and synaptogyrin 1 single and double knockouts.
source: Despite this, the hypothesis that the native function might involve negative regulation of exocytosis has not been pursued extensively, possibly because no clear evidence was found for increases in neurotransmitter release at synapses from synaptophysin 1 and synaptogyrin 1 single and double knockouts (McMahon et al., 1996; Janz et al., 1999; Abraham et al., 2006; Stevens et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Possible compensatory activity of synaptophysin 2 and synaptogyrin 3 has never been assessed in mammals.
source: However, the previous studies, at least in mammals, involved exogenous expression or genetic deletion of synaptophysin 1 and synaptogyrin 1, whereas possible compensatory activity of synaptophysin 2 and synaptogyrin 3 has never been assessed (McInnes et al., 2018).
evidence: This is a statement about the state of prior research, supported by a citation.

claim: QKO mice appeared to develop normally when housed in individually ventilated cages.
source: QKO mice appeared to develop normally when housed in individually ventilated cages, and produced litters of normal size.
evidence: This is an observation from the study.

claim: QKO mice produced litters of normal size.
source: QKO mice appeared to develop normally when housed in individually ventilated cages, and produced litters of normal size.
evidence: This is an observation from the study.

claim: Adult QKO mice were prone to convulsions, sometimes causing death, especially after being startled.
source: However, adults were prone to convulsions, sometimes causing death, especially after being startled.
evidence: This is an observation from the study.

claim: The ventilation system aided survival of QKO mice, possibly by producing continuous white noise that limited startling.
source: We were not able to maintain the colony in a second facility where ventilated cages were not available, suggesting that the ventilation system aided survival, possibly by producing continuous white noise that limited startling.
evidence: This is an inference based on observations of colony maintenance.

claim: A quantitative western blot analysis of homogenized tissue and purified synaptosomes from QKO brains revealed a selective decrease in VAMP 2 levels.
source: A quantitative western blot analysis of homogenized tissue and purified synaptosomes from QKO brains revealed a selective decrease in VAMP 2 levels, but no major changes in a wide variety of other synaptic proteins (Figure 1)
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1.

claim: No major changes in a wide variety of other synaptic proteins were detected in QKO brains.
source: A quantitative western blot analysis of homogenized tissue and purified synaptosomes from QKO brains revealed a selective decrease in VAMP 2 levels, but no major changes in a wide variety of other synaptic proteins (Figure 1)
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1.

claim: A decrease in VAMP 2 levels was detected previously in synaptophysin 1 single knockouts.
source: a decrease in VAMP 2 levels was detected previously in synaptophysin 1 single knockouts (McMahon et al., 1996).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: Calyx of Held synapses from QKO mice were substantially stronger than WT when action potentials were evoked in the afferent axon at low frequency.
source: In a first set of experiments to determine the primary functional deficit, we found that calyx of Held synapses from QKO mice were substantially stronger than WT when action potentials were evoked in the afferent axon at low frequency (Figure 2A–B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A-B.

claim: Excitatory postsynaptic currents (EPSCs) recorded in voltage clamped principal neurons of the medial nucleus of the trapezoid body (MNTB) had a greater quantal content in QKO mice.
source: Excitatory postsynaptic currents (EPSCs) recorded in voltage clamped principal neurons of the medial nucleus of the trapezoid body (MNTB) had a greater quantal content (Figure 2C)
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The synapses were stronger in QKO mice because of exocytosis of transmitter from more presynaptic vesicles.
source: indicating that the synapses were stronger because of exocytosis of transmitter from more presynaptic vesicles, in-line with the presynaptic locus of expression of synaptophysin family members.
evidence: This is an inference based on the greater quantal content and the known presynaptic expression of synaptophysin family members.

claim: Spontaneous quantal release was elevated by a similar amount in QKO mice.
source: Spontaneous quantal release was elevated by a similar amount (Figure 2D–E)
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2D-E.

claim: The size of quantal events was elevated by a smaller amount in QKO mice.
source: and the size of quantal events was elevated by a smaller amount (Figure 2F).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2F.

claim: No significant alterations were detected in the time courses of the EPSCs evoked with low-frequency stimulation or in spontaneous events.
source: No significant alterations were detected in the time courses of the EPSCs evoked with low-frequency stimulation or in spontaneous events (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: The difference in synaptic strength between QKO and WT disappeared quickly, by the 4th action potential during 300Hz stimulation.
source: The difference in synaptic strength disappeared quickly, by the 4th action potential (Figure 3B–C)
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B-C.

claim: There was no difference in the total number of quanta released during the first 150ms of the trains between QKO and WT.
source: and there was no difference in the total number of quanta released during the first 150ms of the trains (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: 150ms is enough to nearly completely exhaust the RRP at calyx of Held synapses.
source: The result suggests that the RRP content was not altered at QKO synapses because 150ms is enough to nearly completely exhaust the RRP (Mahfooz et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: The RRP content was not altered at QKO synapses.
source: The result suggests that the RRP content was not altered at QKO synapses because 150ms is enough to nearly completely exhaust the RRP (Mahfooz et al., 2016).
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental data and prior knowledge.

claim: The mean probability of release per vesicle (p̄v) was approximately double at QKO synapses.
source: In contrast, p¯v is calculated by dividing the number of quanta released after isolated action potentials by the RRP content, and was approximately double at QKO synapses (Figure 3E).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: Removing synaptophysin family members increased the value of p̄v without altering RRP content.
source: These results show that removing synaptophysin family members increased the value of p¯v without altering RRP content.
evidence: This is a summary of the experimental findings.

claim: Endogenous synaptophysin family members inhibit neurotransmission downstream of vesicle recruitment to the RRP.
source: Taken together, they suggest that endogenous synaptophysin family members inhibit neurotransmission downstream of vesicle recruitment to the RRP.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental findings.

claim: No deficits were seen in the rate at which vesicles are recruited to the RRP at later times during the trains of 300 Hz stimulation at QKO synapses.
source: If so, removing family members would have produced a deficit in the rate at which vesicles are recruited to the RRP at later times during the trains of 300 Hz stimulation, which drove multiple rounds of exocytosis (see Legend of Figure 3D), and during subsequent rest intervals. But no such deficits were seen at QKO synapses.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Figures 3-4.

claim: All methods produced matching estimates for vesicle recruitment during heavy use for QKO and WT synapses.
source: All produced matching estimates for QKO and WT synapses (Figure 3F)
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3F.

claim: Steady state quantal output after the 150th ms of 300 Hz stimulation was similar at QKO synapses compared to WT.
source: The absence of a deficit in recruitment during extended stimulation could additionally be deduced without referencing any of the methods simply from the observation that steady state quantal output after the 150th ms of 300 Hz stimulation was similar at QKO synapses compared to WT (53.4 ± 4.7 quanta/action potential vs 59.2 ± 11.7).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data.

claim: No alteration was found in the timing of RRP replenishment during rest intervals that followed 300 Hz stimulation.
source: Nor did we find any alteration in the timing of RRP replenishment during rest intervals that followed 300 Hz stimulation (Figure 4).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4.

claim: The results do not support the hypothesis that synaptophysin family members play a critical post-exocytosis role in facilitating ongoing vesicle priming and release at calyx of Held synapses.
source: These results do not support the hypothesis that synaptophysin family members play a critical post-exocytosis role in facilitating ongoing vesicle priming and release, at least at calyx of Held synapses.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental findings.

claim: Some readily releasable vesicles are released more slowly than others during repetitive stimulation owing to a lower probability of release.
source: That is, the initial idea was that the RRP is a homogeneous pool (Elmqvist and Quastel, 1965; Vere-Jones, 1966), but there is now widespread agreement that some readily releasable vesicles are released more slowly than others during repetitive stimulation owing to a lower probability of release (Wu and Borst, 1999; Sakaba and Neher, 2001; Moulder and Mennerick, 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Both high and low pv vesicles seem to be immediately releasable at the calyx of Held.
source: Both high and low pv vesicles seem to be immediately releasable, at least in the calyx of Held preparation examined here, and the timing of exocytosis is tightly synchronized to action potentials (Mahfooz et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior literature and experimental data in the current study.

claim: The timing of exocytosis is tightly synchronized to action potentials at the calyx of Held.
source: Both high and low pv vesicles seem to be immediately releasable, at least in the calyx of Held preparation examined here, and the timing of exocytosis is tightly synchronized to action potentials (Mahfooz et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior literature and experimental data in the current study.

claim: All methods produced p̄v values for the vesicles remaining in the RRP that were higher for QKO synapses compared to WT.
source: However, all methods produced p¯v values for the vesicles remaining in the RRP that were higher for QKO synapses compared to WT (Figure 5E).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5E.

claim: The p̄v values for both WT and QKO were approximately 3-fold lower during 50 or 100 Hz stimulation compared to the corresponding values when the RRP was full.
source: The p¯v values for both WT and QKO were approximately 3-fold lower during 50 or 100 Hz stimulation compared to the corresponding values when the RRP was full (compare Figure 5E to Figure 3E), confirming that high pv vesicles were eliminated.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 5E and 3E.

claim: Almost all of the vesicles remaining within the RRP during both 50 and 100 Hz stimulation were in the low pv state.
source: And indeed, almost all of the vesicles remaining within the RRP during both 50 and 100 Hz stimulation must have been in the low pv state because 100 Hz stimulation depleted the RRP to a greater extent (Figure 5—figure supplement 2), but did not further lower the value for p¯v (Figure 5E).
evidence: This is an inference based on experimental data shown in Figures 5E and Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: Synaptophysin family members inhibit exocytosis of low and high pv vesicles alike.
source: These results do not distinguish between the classes of models with single and multiple sequential vesicle priming steps mentioned above, but do indicate that synaptophysin family members inhibit exocytosis of low and high pv vesicles alike.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental findings.

claim: Synaptophysin family members inhibit neurotransmission downstream of the final step in vesicle priming.
source: The results therefore strongly suggest that family members inhibit neurotransmission downstream of the final step in vesicle priming, which is consistent with the increase in spontaneous exocytosis seen in the absence of action potentials documented in Figure 2D–E.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental findings.

claim: Postsynaptic responses depressed more rapidly at QKO Schaffer collateral synapses compared to WT.
source: Nevertheless, similar to at the calyx of Held, postsynaptic responses depressed more rapidly at QKO synapses compared to WT (Figure 6B–C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6B-C.

claim: A kinetic analysis indicated that p̄v was approximately double at Schaffer collateral synapses from QKO mice.
source: A kinetic analysis indicated that p¯v was approximately double (Figure 6D–E)
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6D-E.

claim: The timing of vesicle recruitment to the RRP during ongoing stimulation was not altered at Schaffer collateral synapses from QKO mice.
source: whereas the timing of vesicle recruitment to the RRP during ongoing stimulation was not altered (Figure 6F).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6F.

claim: No difference was detected in the time course of RRP replenishment during subsequent rest intervals at Schaffer collateral synapses from QKO mice.
source: And, no difference was detected in the time course of RRP replenishment during subsequent rest intervals (Figure 6G).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6G.

claim: The machinery that catalyzes synaptic vesicle exocytosis becomes more efficient after removing synaptophysin family proteins at hippocampal synapses.
source: These results extend to hippocampal synapses the conclusion that the machinery that catalyzes synaptic vesicle exocytosis becomes more efficient after removing synaptophysin family proteins, whereas the timing of vesicle recruitment to the RRP is not altered.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental findings.

claim: Schaffer collateral synapses are typically used at frequencies that are ∼15-fold lower than calyx of Held synapses in nature.
source: The comparison between calyces of Held and Schaffer collateral synapses is a good test for generality across synapse types because, in nature, Schaffer collateral synapses are typically used at frequencies that are ∼15-fold lower in addition to striking morphological and molecular differences and the ∼20-fold difference in the timing of vesicle trafficking already noted above (Ranck, 1973; Hermann et al., 2007; Borst and Soria van Hoeve, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: There is a ∼20-fold difference in the timing of vesicle trafficking between calyx of Held and Schaffer collateral synapses.
source: The comparison between calyces of Held and Schaffer collateral synapses is a good test for generality across synapse types because, in nature, Schaffer collateral synapses are typically used at frequencies that are ∼15-fold lower in addition to striking morphological and molecular differences and the ∼20-fold difference in the timing of vesicle trafficking already noted above (Ranck, 1973; Hermann et al., 2007; Borst and Soria van Hoeve, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature and experimental data in the current study.

claim: QKO synapses destained almost 2-fold more than WT during 0.2 Hz stimulation in the FM4-64 assay.
source: And indeed, QKO synapses destained almost 2-fold more than WT during the 0.2 Hz stimulation (Figure 7A–C), confirming that p¯v is elevated.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7A-C.

claim: No differences were detected during 20 Hz stimulation in the FM4-64 assay between QKO and WT.
source: And, no differences were detected during subsequent 20 Hz stimulation (not shown), or during 20 Hz stimulation when the 0.2 Hz train was omitted (Figure 7D), confirming that the timing of vesicle recruitment to the RRP was not altered.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7D.

claim: No differences between QKO and WT were detected in the amount of staining during loading in the FM4-64 assay.
source: Furthermore, no differences between QKO and WT were detected in the amount of staining during loading, further supporting the conclusion of no alterations in rate-limiting steps in vesicle trafficking in QKO synapses.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data.

claim: Synaptophysin 1 or synaptogyrin 3 alone largely compensated for the loss of the other three family members.
source: Of the triple knockouts lacking all but one of the neuronal family members, synaptophysin 1 or synaptogyrin 3 alone largely compensated for the loss of the other three family members (Figure 7C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7C.

claim: Synapses from triple knockouts expressing only synaptophysin 2 were not noticeably different from QKO.
source: Intriguingly, synapses from triple knockouts expressing only synaptophysin 2 were not noticeably different from QKO
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7C.

claim: The combination of synaptophysin 2 with either synaptophysin 1 or synaptogyrin 3 was less effective at compensation than synaptophysin 1 or synaptogyrin 3 alone.
source: but the combination of synaptophysin 2 with either synaptophysin 1 or synaptogyrin 3 was less effective at compensation than synaptophysin 1 or synaptogyrin 3 alone (Figure 7E).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7E.

claim: Synaptophysin 2 may act as a competitive inhibitor of the function of other family members, or play a dominant negative role.
source: This result suggests that synaptophysin 2 may act as a competitive inhibitor of the function of other family members, or play a dominant negative role.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental findings.

claim: Synaptophysin 2 is unique in that it lacks many of the sites for C-terminal tyrosine phosphorylation that are striking features of the other family members.
source: And indeed, synaptophysin 2 is unique in that it lacks many of the sites for C-terminal tyrosine phosphorylation that are striking features of the other family members (Evans and Cousin, 2005).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: Synaptophysin family proteins are widely expressed in synaptic vesicle membranes, with more individuals per vesicle than the extensively studied synaptotagmins.
source: Synaptophysin family proteins are widely expressed in synaptic vesicle membranes, with more individuals per vesicle than the extensively studied synaptotagmins, although likely less than the vSNARE VAMP 2 and homologs (Takamori et al., 2006; Wilhelm et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: The efficiency of the release machinery is elevated at a variety of synapse types from knockout mice where all four neuronal family members have been deleted.
source: Here, we show that the efficiency of the release machinery is elevated at a variety of synapse types from knockout mice where all four neuronal family members have been deleted, with no indication of any alteration in RRP content or the timing of vesicle recruitment to the RRP during light or heavy use.
evidence: This is a summary of the experimental findings.

claim: The new results strongly suggest that synaptophysin family members modulate function at the level of exocytosis.
source: The new results strongly suggest that synaptophysin family members modulate function at the level of exocytosis.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental findings.

claim: The native action of synaptophysin family members likely includes inhibition.
source: If so, the native action likely includes inhibition, especially when the results are taken together with an earlier study where exogenous synaptophysin 1 and synaptogyrin 1 potently inhibited exocytosis (Sugita et al., 1999; but see Alder et al., 1995).
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental findings and prior literature.

claim: The alteration in QKO synapses is unusually specific.
source: First, the alteration is unusually specific; p¯v was elevated without desynchronizing the relationship between action potentials and neurotransmitter release, or disrupting other vesicle trafficking mechanisms that control presynaptic function such as the capacity of the RRP for storing synaptic vesicles and the timing of vesicle recruitment to vacancies within the RRP.
evidence: This is a summary of the experimental findings.

claim: The alteration was robust across a variety of synapse types embedded within neuronal networks that are subject to dissimilar developmental forces.
source: Second, the alteration was robust across a variety of synapse types embedded within neuronal networks that are subject to dissimilar developmental forces, including the networks formed by neurons grown in dissociated cell culture.
evidence: This is a summary of the experimental findings.

claim: Besides the decrease in VAMP 2, no substantial changes in levels of a variety of other proteins implicated in exocytosis were detected.
source: Third, besides the decrease in VAMP 2, we did not detect substantial changes in levels of a variety of other proteins that have been implicated in exocytosis, including syntaxin 1, SNAP-25, RIM 1/2, Munc13-1, Rab 3a, and complexin 1/2.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1.

claim: Synaptophysin 2 seemed to inhibit the function of other family members.
source: And fourth, synaptophysin 2 seemed to inhibit the function of other family members, which argues against the specific concern that removing the other family members increased the fusogenicity of synaptic vesicles mechanically, by simply exposing space on the surface vesicular membranes.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental findings.

claim: No elevation in p̄v was detected in neuromuscular junctions after deleting the family from C. elegans or Drosophila.
source: Notably, however, no elevation in p¯v was detected in neuromuscular junctions after deleting the family from C. elegans or Drosophila - and exocytosis of neurotransmitter was increased rather than decreased after expressing exogenous synaptophysin 1 in Xenopus - and it seems unlikely that an entire family of proteins would have an unrelated function in the different species (Alder et al., 1995; Abraham et al., 2006; Stevens et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Exocytosis of neurotransmitter was increased rather than decreased after expressing exogenous synaptophysin 1 in Xenopus.
source: Notably, however, no elevation in p¯v was detected in neuromuscular junctions after deleting the family from C. elegans or Drosophila - and exocytosis of neurotransmitter was increased rather than decreased after expressing exogenous synaptophysin 1 in Xenopus - and it seems unlikely that an entire family of proteins would have an unrelated function in the different species (Alder et al., 1995; Abraham et al., 2006; Stevens et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Family members might function as bi-directional regulators of exocytosis where the directionality is modulated by second messengers, possibly via phosphorylation of the tyrosine residues along the C-terminal tail.
source: One possibility is that family members function as bi-directional regulators of exocytosis where the directionality is modulated by second messengers, possibly via phosphorylation of the tyrosine residues along the C-terminal tail.
evidence: This is speculation about possible mechanisms.

claim: When bound to synaptophysin 1, VAMP 2 was excluded from the core SNARE complex consisting of VAMP 2, syntaxin 1, and SNAP25 that catalyzes exocytosis.
source: However, when bound to synaptophysin 1, VAMP 2 was excluded from the core SNARE complex consisting of VAMP 2, syntaxin 1, and SNAP25 that catalyzes exocytosis (Edelmann et al., 1995)
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: The combination of syntaxin 1 and SNAP25 could disrupt the binding between synaptophysin 1 and VAMP 2 in an enriched vesicle preparation.
source: and the combination of syntaxin 1 and SNAP25 could disrupt the binding between synaptophysin 1 and VAMP 2 in an enriched vesicle preparation (Siddiqui et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: Lowering levels of the SNAP-25 component paradoxically increased p̄v in at least one study.
source: However, we are not aware of evidence that exocytosis can be modulated in this manner, and indeed, lowering levels of the SNAP-25 component paradoxically increased p¯v in at least one study (Antonucci et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: Exogenous VAMP 2 could be driven to synaptic vesicles by co-expressing synaptophysin 1.
source: Intriguingly, the reduction is in-line with a previous study where exogenous VAMP 2 could be driven to synaptic vesicles by co-expressing synaptophysin 1 (Pennuto et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: The results do not suggest that synaptophysin family members are required for targeting VAMP 2 to synaptic vesicles.
source: The results do not suggest that synaptophysin family members are required for targeting VAMP 2 to synaptic vesicles
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental findings.

claim: It is possible that VAMP 2 exists in two pools within vesicle membranes: one of which is stabilized by binding to synaptophysin family members; and the other by a different factor that remains to be identified.
source: but are consistent with the possibility that VAMP 2 exists in two pools within vesicle membranes: one of which is stabilized by binding to synaptophysin family members; and the other by a different factor that remains to be identified.
evidence: This is speculation based on the experimental findings.

claim: It is possible that the reduction in VAMP 2 in QKO synaptosomes resulted from depletion from plasma membrane rather than synaptic vesicles.
source: On the other hand, it is possible that the reduction in QKO synaptosomes resulted from depletion from plasma membrane rather than synaptic vesicles because significant amounts of VAMP 2 are consistently found in plasma membranes (Sankaranarayanan et al., 2000), and synaptosomes contain plasma membrane in addition to synaptic vesicles.
evidence: This is speculation based on prior knowledge.

claim: Vesicles were larger in Drosophila synaptogyrin mutants.
source: We cannot rule out a postsynaptic mechanism, but vesicles were larger in the Drosophila mutants, which might play a role.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior literature (Stevens et al., 2012).

claim: Vesicles were larger in synapses from knockouts of other presynaptic proteins involved in exocytosis, including VAMP 2, SNAP-25, and Munc13-1/2.
source: Possibly also relevant: Vesicles were also larger in synapses from knockouts of other presynaptic proteins involved in exocytosis, including VAMP 2, SNAP-25, and Munc13-1/2; the increase in radius was <10%, but even this small increase would translate to an increase in volume of 30%, which is more than the elevation in quantal size seen here (Imig et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: The decreased paired-pulse facilitation and increased paired-pulse depression seen in single, double and quadruple knockouts may result from the baseline elevation of p̄v.
source: However, the decreased paired-pulse facilitation and increased paired-pulse depression seen in single, double and quadruple knockouts at a variety of synapse types do not necessarily indicate defects in mechanisms underlying short-term plasticity, but instead may result from the baseline elevation of p¯v.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental findings.

claim: Paired-pulse facilitation could be unmasked at QKO synapses by lowering extracellular Ca2+.
source: And indeed, paired-pulse facilitation could be unmasked at QKO synapses by lowering extracellular Ca2+, which lowers the baseline (Figure 8).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 8.

claim: The elevation in p̄v at QKO synapses cannot be attributed solely to the superpriming phenomenon.
source: In any case, the elevation in p¯v at QKO synapses cannot be attributed solely to the superpriming phenomenon proposed in Taschenberger et al. (2016) because the frequency jump experiments documented in Figure 5 indicated that the elevated release probability pertained to both low and high pv vesicles, whereas superpriming is thought to pertain exclusively to vesicles with high pv.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental findings and prior literature.

claim: The evidence against substantial deficits in the timing of vesicle recruitment to the RRP at QKO synapses seems to be strong.
source: The evidence against substantial deficits in the timing of vesicle recruitment to the RRP at QKO synapses seems to be strong.
evidence: This is a summary of the experimental findings.

claim: Receptor desensitization mechanisms that could occlude differences between QKO and WT in the electrophysiological studies were ruled out with additional experiments.
source: In particular, receptor desensitization mechanisms that could occlude differences between QKO and WT in the electrophysiological studies were ruled out with additional experiments in Figure 3—figure supplement 1 for calyx of Held and in Wesseling et al. (2002) for Schaffer collateral synapses.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1 and a citation to prior literature.
